title: Private Set Intersection Mule Graph for Credit Unions
one_liner: Let hundreds of small banks and credit unions ask 'has anyone flagged this payee account?' without revealing customers or lists, using cryptographic private set intersection.
customer: Credit unions and community banks, sold through CUSOs, leagues and core processors, plus fintech sponsor banks.
problem: One account takeover can send 50+ ACH transfers to accounts at multiple banks, and each bank sees only its slice. Large-institution consortia dominate, and smaller institutions avoid sharing because of privacy, liability and competitive-leakage worries, even though information-sharing rules (314(b)) allow it.
solution: A pre-payment check API and core-integration widget. A payee's hashed account and routing data is checked via private set intersection against the pool of accounts members have flagged, returning hit count, recency and fraud category without exposing either side's lists. It adds burst alerts that notify other members when a takeover is in progress and automates the compliance paperwork.
why_now: Open-source PSI libraries and confidential-compute services have matured. The FBI freeze data exposed the cross-bank blind spot, Socure's $5.2B valuation shows the market's value, and FedNow adoption is reaching smaller institutions.
revenue_model: $500-5K per month per institution by asset size, and per-check fees for fintechs.
non_obvious_insight: Banks decline to share data because of liability and competitive leakage, not indifference. Cryptography removes the objection without asking anyone to trust a vendor with their data, and the network effect is regional, so a single state league can seed it.
first_30_days: Talk to a state credit-union league and recruit 5 pilot credit unions. Seed with confirmed-fraud lists they already hold, build the API on open-source PSI, and sign letters of intent for paid rollout.

title: Pre-Cut Electrical Kits Per House Plan
one_liner: A regional kitting shop ships each production home's wiring as pre-cut, labeled, bundled kits so a helper pulls and a journeyman only terminates and inspects.
customer: Electrical subcontractors serving production and spec builders (5-100 homes a year), and builders in data-center-hot markets such as Texas.
problem: Data centers absorb electricians (nearly a third of the shortage; journeymen on overtime gross $130-170K, vendor stat), and Texas builders report electrical delays of up to 2 months. Meanwhile much rough-in time goes to measuring, cutting and pulling, which does not need a licensed person's minutes.
solution: For each repeat plan, generate a wire schedule and build kits: cable pre-cut and labeled by room and circuit, boxes pre-assembled, home runs pre-bundled, panel schedule pre-printed, delivered in numbered bins by phase. Lower-skill pullers or apprentices do most of the rough-in under supervision, and the journeyman terminates and inspects.
why_now: Electrician arbitrage from data-center overtime, builders with idle houses waiting on electrical, and digital plan libraries that expose structured circuit data. Wire-processing machines are cheap and used equipment is plentiful.
revenue_model: Materials plus 15-25%, or $2-4K per home, with a share of labor savings. Licensing the process to kitting shops in other metros.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is journeyman minutes on tasks a journeyman does not need to do. Commercial contractors have prefabbed for decades, but residential never did because labor was cheap, and now the ROI is large.
first_30_days: Pick one production builder's most repeated plan. Hire an ex-electrician estimator and buy or rent a used cut-and-label machine. Sell kits for five homes to the builder's electrical sub and measure hours saved per house.

title: Shared Emergency Desk for Autonomous Fleets
one_liner: A neutral 24/7 first-responder interface (hotline, dispatch API, geofence directives) that small AV, robot-truck and delivery-robot operators rent instead of building.
customer: Newer and second-tier AV operators (autonomous trucking, shuttles, delivery pods, robotaxi entrants), and city and county 911 dispatch centers on the public-facing side.
problem: Regulators are asking for a human phone number, not more autonomy. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on July 8, 2026, and California's AV enforcement rules take effect in 2026 (as I understand them). Waymo alone runs about 70 remote agents per shift from two centers in the Philippines, which small operators cannot copy.
solution: A US-staffed desk trained on fire and police protocols. It offers standardized emergency-response guides, one API through which dispatch centers can stop, unlock or reroute any subscribing fleet, compliance logs, and drills for first responders.
why_now: Driverless trucking is commercial (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k driverless orders, Einride listed), new AV entrants are launching, and states are writing rules. Compliance deadlines land in 2026.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per vehicle per year or an $8-25k monthly fleet retainer, plus training contracts with cities.
non_obvious_insight: A commodity BPO with liability attached scales with vehicle count, and neutrality is a feature because cities prefer one interface for all fleets. Large operators build their own desks, so the long tail of new entrants is the market.
first_30_days: Interview 10 safety and compliance leads at autonomous trucking and delivery-robot companies. Build a minimal hotline plus web console for a single pilot, co-design the protocol with 2 city or county dispatch centers, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $5k a month.

title: Human Failover Retainer for Agent-Run Businesses
one_liner: Backup-generator economics for know-how: a retained, drilled bench of human operators that takes over within hours when a company's AI agents fail.
customer: Owners and COOs of 10-200 person companies that replaced back-office headcount with AI agents. First niche: freight brokerages (dispatch, carrier onboarding, load booking). Then medical billing firms, property managers, insurance agencies and 3PLs.
problem: After automation, the people who knew the manual process leave. Then a model deprecation, provider outage, prompt regression, API key ban or payment-processor freeze halts revenue, and nobody remembers how to do the job by hand. Cloud disaster-recovery plans protect servers, not the tacit process knowledge. That skill decays every month the automation succeeds.
solution: A $1.5-6k/month retainer. Phase 1: shadow the process while it still lives in staff heads and write executable runbooks and checklists. Phase 2: keep a pre-vetted bench of remote operators (ex-dispatchers, ex-billers) who sample live work weekly, so they stay current. Phase 3: run quarterly 'lights-out drills' that switch the agents off for four hours and measure time to recover. Guarantee takeover within two hours, billed hourly on activation. The bench's weekly sampling doubles as gold-label QA that flags agent drift, so the retainer also improves the agents.
why_now: 2025-26 brought large cloud and LLM-API outages (for example the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 incident), fast model deprecation cycles, and boards booking headcount cuts on the strength of agents. Insurers are starting to ask about AI-related business-interruption exposure, which gives a compliance reason to buy.
revenue_model: Monthly retainer tiered by process criticality; activation fees at $60-120 per operator-hour; drill and runbook-documentation fees; an insurer or broker referral channel that offers premium credits for a documented failover plan.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody buys a generator until the blackout, but unlike a generator the failover gets more expensive the more successful the AI rollout is, because human know-how atrophies. The best time to sell is right after a company celebrates automation savings, and the CFO can fund the retainer out of those savings. It is a services business that looks like insurance, with recurring revenue, and a bench of a few dozen part-timers can cover many clients.
first_30_days: Pick freight brokerage and find 40 brokers advertising AI dispatch or quoting. Offer a free two-hour 'lights-out drill' to about 10 of them: switch off the agents, time the recovery and hand back a one-page automation-debt score. Recruit 6 part-time ex-dispatchers as the bench. Convert 3 drill participants to $1.5-2.5k/month retainers. Package the outputs as a case study.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Downstream Buyers
one_liner: Importers of record are collecting over $100B in tariff refunds, but the small businesses that paid tariff surcharges on their invoices are owed a share and nobody is collecting it for them.
customer: Mid-size US contractors, restaurant groups, retailers and manufacturers ($5M-$200M revenue) whose 2025-26 supplier invoices carried explicit tariff surcharges or tariff-attributed price increases.
problem: Refunds go to the importer of record, and many importers already passed the cost through. Downstream buyers may have contract or unjust-enrichment claims, but their AP teams never tracked surcharges. Small importers also find filing costly ('not without a cost,' Colorado Sun, 2026-07-02), so cash sits with parties who have no incentive to share it.
solution: Connect to QuickBooks, NetSuite or the AP inbox and extract every invoice line mentioning a tariff or surcharge. Map each vendor to its importer of record using public import records. Estimate the refund-attributable share and generate demand packets with contract citations. A partner law firm handles escalations on contingency. Default settlement is a vendor credit memo, which preserves the relationship.
why_now: More than $100B has been refunded (CNBC 2026-08-07, Forbes 2026-09-09), the government is fighting an order to refund all importers (WaPo 2026-08-11), tariff lawsuits are surging, and 25 states are challenging the replacement Section 122 tariffs. That means a second wave of surcharges to track.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered cash or credits. After the first recovery, $299-$999 per month SaaS to track surcharges and refund clauses on future tariff swings.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is watching who receives the refund, and nobody watches who funded it. Many invoices literally say 'tariff surcharge, pass-through.' Vendors prefer credit memos to cash, so recoveries can be quiet and relationship-safe. The same invoice-clause tooling becomes a permanent tariff-swing shield.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 SMBs through trade associations and small-business communities and pull 24 months of AP exports. Run the analysis by hand with a lawyer's template letter and produce a $1M aggregate identified-claim demo. Sign two contingent agreements and send the first ten demand letters.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

title: Safety Compliance-as-a-Service for Robot Deployments
one_liner: A standing team plus software that produces the risk assessments, safety validation and insurer paperwork every facility needs before deploying AMRs, cobots or humanoid pilots.
customer: EHS and operations directors at mid-size 3PLs, manufacturers and food or cold-storage plants, integrators without in-house safety staff, and insurers who want documentation.
problem: Deployments stall at safety sign-off. ISO 10218 was revised in 2025, standards for dynamically stable robots and humanoids are still being written, integrators are overloaded, and insurers and OSHA ask for documented assessments. Amazon's 1M-robot scale keeps injury scrutiny high.
solution: Field engineers plus templated software: site scan, risk assessment against current standards, laser-scanner zone and e-stop validation, speed-and-separation testing, training records and incident logs, with annual recertification. Offer a premium 'humanoid pilot safety case' product.
why_now: Humanoid pilots are moving into real facilities in 2026 (Figure reports about 350 units delivered, Agility has a $300M+ single-customer order) while standards lag. Insurers are starting to require paperwork, so it is a channel as well as a service.
revenue_model: $8-25k per site assessment, $3-8k a year for recertification, and software seats for integrators.
non_obvious_insight: For many humanoid and AMR pilots the true bottleneck is one safety officer's signature, and almost no independent practitioners exist. Insurers will steer clients to whoever produces accepted documentation, which gives you distribution.
first_30_days: Recruit a certified functional-safety engineer as cofounder and build assessment templates. Sell 3 fixed-price assessments at about $10k each from integrators' backlogs, and publish a free humanoid pilot safety checklist to generate inbound.

title: Publish the Obvious: Generative Prior Art vs. Patent Thickets
one_liner: Turn cheap AI generation into a defensive weapon by industrially publishing dated, enabling disclosures of every obvious variant around a product, so secondary 'evergreening' and troll patents can't be granted.
customer: Primary: generic and biosimilar manufacturers and public-interest funders (procurement agencies, health-access NGOs) facing secondary patent thickets on drugs losing primary protection. Secondary: hardware, robotics and protocol-foundation startups afraid of patent trolls.
problem: Secondary patents on dosing regimens, polymorphs, formulations, devices and manufacturing tweaks extend monopolies long after the core compound expires, and they are cheap to file, especially now that AI drafts applications. Challengers' tools (IPR, oppositions, litigation) are expensive and come after the patent issues. Startups have no defense budget against troll assertions.
solution: A pipeline in which LLMs plus a patent agent or PhD reviewer enumerate the design space around a target product: formulations, dose schedules, salt and crystal forms, delivery devices, process variations. It drafts enabling defensive disclosures and timestamps them. It deposits them where examiners actually search (IP.com Prior Art Database, Research Disclosure, plus DOI-bearing repositories such as Zenodo and ChemRxiv that patent-office non-patent-literature tools crawl). It then monitors new filings, maps which disclosures block which claims, and files third-party submissions where the law allows. Sold as a per-product 'novelty shield' with measurable outcomes: examiner citations and rejections.
why_now: Compound patents on semaglutide and other blockbuster GLP-1s are expiring in several large markets in 2026, triggering a stampede of generic entry and follow-on patent strategies. LLMs now make it cheap to enumerate enabling variants at scale. Patent offices are swamped and revising guidance on AI-assisted work, and nobody has industrialized the defensive side of the novelty game.
revenue_model: $15-80k per product-family shield for generics and funders; $500-2k/month subscriptions for startups and foundations; success-based bonuses when a filing is rejected citing a disclosure; grant and NGO funding for public-health targets.
non_obvious_insight: Prior-art status depends on what was publicly and enablingly disclosed, not on who or what wrote it. So when generating variations is free, the asymmetric weapon is to publish the space before anyone can claim it. The scarce thing is no longer ideas but credible, discoverable, dated publication. It also aligns the incentive: the parties who pay (generics, health funders) gain directly from the commons staying open.
first_30_days: Pick 3 products with visible secondary-patent thickets and imminent generic entry. Produce about 200 enabling disclosures per product, each reviewed by a contracted patent agent. Publish to two or three searchable indexes. Send free 'thicket map' reports to 5 generic makers and 2 access-focused funders. Sell the first shield for $15-25k. Track later filings to prove examiner citations. Have patent counsel vet the approach up front, including that every disclosure is actually enabling and accurate.

title: Referee Sampling for Black Mass and Battery Scrap
one_liner: Independent sampling and assay of black mass lots, using Pierre Gy's Theory of Sampling from mining, so scrap sellers and recyclers stop fighting over 5-15% payable swings.
customer: Battery-scrap sellers who are paid by assay: gigafactory scrap desks, EV and ESS dismantlers, and shredder pre-processors in Germany, Poland, the US Midwest, Ontario and Korea. Buyers are hydromet recyclers and trading houses that want defensible acceptance. Whoever needs the settlement pays $1.5-4k per lot or $15-40 per tonne, and often splits it.
problem: Black mass is a worst-case heterogeneous powder: coarse Cu and Al foil flakes, plastic, residual electrolyte, graphite, and a nugget effect for Ni, Co and Cu. Payables are computed on the assay of a few grams. Anyone from mining knows 90% or more of assay error is sampling error (fundamental, segregation and grouping errors), not lab error. Sellers and buyers each sample their own way and get 5-15% differences on Ni, Co and Li. Disputes are settled by splitting the difference or sending to an 'umpire' lab that repeats the same bad sampling. On a $60-150k lot, that swing is $5-15k of pure noise, paid to whoever wins the argument. The industry's chemists treat it like a homogeneous chemical.
solution: Build a containerised, safety-rated sampling and sample-prep station (dryer, rotary divider, splitter, pulverizer, inert handling) and a written ToS-based protocol: incremental sampling from a falling stream or drum auger, particle-size and moisture control, and duplicate-sample bias checks. Send splits to an accredited lab and issue a 'referee certificate' with a stated sampling variance. Provide a two-line settlement clause template that buyer and seller adopt (for example, 'referee result binds') and tie lot IDs to the recycled-content and material-recovery documentation the EU Battery Regulation requires. Extend later to PCB e-waste, catalyst scrap and mixed copper scrap.
why_now: Black mass volumes are ramping with European and US gigafactory ramp-up scrap (often 10-30% early yield loss). EU regulation is pushing black mass toward hazardous-waste treatment and export limits, and Battery Regulation recovery and recycled-content rules are phasing in. Several Western recyclers restructured or were bought out in 2025 (Li-Cycle into Glencore, for example), so sellers now fear counterparty and assay risk. Payables have become the main margin lever as Co and Ni prices swing.
revenue_model: Per-lot referee fee ($1.5-4k) or $15-40 per tonne, annual retainers for large scrap generators, leasing or operating sample-prep stations at recycler gates, and certification and training for recyclers' in-house sampling.
non_obvious_insight: The fight looks like an assay-accuracy problem but it is a sampling problem, and the solution is 1950s-1990s sampling theory that only mining and metallurgy people internalise. Recycling companies are staffed by chemists and process engineers who sample like it is a solution. A person who has been burned by a bad grade-control sample sees the whole market as one giant unsampled stockpile.
first_30_days: Rent time on a commercial sample-prep lab or buy used splitting and pulverizing gear (about $40-60k). Offer a free duplicate-sampling study to three scrap generators or dismantlers: take 10 lots, sample each with the seller's method and yours, and send blind splits to two labs. Show them the between-protocol bias, then sell a 6-month referee retainer. A local mining-lab partner and one senior sampling consultant give instant credibility.

title: Programmable Lockbox for GPU and Robot Collateral
one_liner: Tri-party custody software and hardware that lets lenders verify, and if needed take over, financed GPU clusters and robot fleets sitting in someone else's building.
customer: Specialty and private-credit lenders and equipment lessors financing GPU clouds and robots-as-a-service. Borrowers such as neoclouds and robot operators pay to lower their borrowing spread, and colo operators act as a channel.
problem: More than $20B of loans are now secured by GPUs, and H100-class rental rates fell from about $7-10 per hour in early 2024 to $2-4 by late 2025, so lenders must know whether machines exist, are powered and utilised, and are not double-pledged. Monitoring today is a spreadsheet plus quarterly audits. The bigger trapdoors are the colo landlord's lien for unpaid power or rent and who physically or remotely controls the hardware on default.
solution: (1) A continuous collateral-health feed: hardware serials and attestation (TPM or GPU attestation where available), BMC and out-of-band data, power-meter readings, latency-based geolocation, and periodic photo audits by colo remote hands. (2) Escrowed step-in credentials for BMC and fleet consoles, plus a tri-party lockbox agreement with the colo covering access and lien waivers, with API-triggered 'freeze' and 'transfer to lender' modes. (3) Standard borrowing-base reports.
why_now: GPU-collateralised private credit scaled from almost nothing to over $20B in about two years, with loans maturing 2026-2028 among a small, correlated lender group. Banks avoid the fast-depreciating collateral, leaving private credit to fill the gap. Utilisation and location risk is now board-level for lenders. Robot-as-a-service leasing needs the same control layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per GPU or robot per month paid by the borrower, or 10-25 bps on outstanding facility size, plus a $25k onboarding fee per facility and colo referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Lender losses come from control failures such as liens, access and double-pledging, not from chips vanishing. Contracts plus access-control APIs solve most of it. The borrower is the real buyer, because a 50-100 bps lower spread beats the fee, so sell it to the neocloud CFO as a rate reduction.
first_30_days: Speak with 15 specialty lenders and equipment-finance boutiques and 10 GPU-cloud CFOs. Sell a manual 'collateral control audit' at $15-30k for two facilities. Draft the tri-party lockbox template with a finance lawyer, then productise the attestation feed.

title: Security Grant Desk for Small Congregations
one_liner: Flat-fee application, vulnerability-assessment and post-award compliance packages for small houses of worship using FEMA's Nonprofit Security Grant Program and state equivalents.
customer: Small synagogues, mosques, churches, gurdwaras and temples, and umbrella bodies such as federations, dioceses and mosque councils.
problem: FY2026 NSGP offered $300M (notice published 24 June 2026, deadline extended to 24 July) at up to $200k per site. Applications need a vulnerability assessment, an investment justification and SAM.gov and UEI registration. Small congregations lack the administrative capacity, and post-award procurement and reimbursement rules trip them.
solution: Templated assessments built on CISA's free self-assessment, an investment-justification drafting workflow with security-vendor quote gathering, SAM and UEI onboarding, a state-agency deadline tracker, and post-award procurement and reimbursement compliance. Flat fees only, because FEMA guidance generally bars contingent-fee grant writing.
why_now: FY2026 awards are being announced now and FY2027 prep starts this fall. Threat levels keep congregations motivated.
revenue_model: $1.5-4k per application, $800 for post-award compliance, and $150/month trackers for federations.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier is administrative capacity, not eligibility, and referrals flow through community federations. Post-award compliance is the neglected second revenue stream.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 regional federations or mosque councils, run free FY2027-prep webinars, and sell 10 assessment packages. Build a network of vetted security installers for quotes.

title: Metering Unmetered Wells From Orbit
one_liner: Estimate monthly pumping for every unmetered irrigation well by fusing radar subsidence, satellite crop water use and electricity data, and sell it to groundwater regulators.
customer: Groundwater sustainability agencies (about 140 in California), Texas groundwater conservation districts, Kansas management districts and Arizona active management areas, plus ag lenders, farmland funds and data-center developers relying on groundwater. Agencies pay annual fees.
problem: Most irrigation wells are unmetered, so regulators cannot enforce pumping limits or fees. Broad drought and Colorado River cuts push more pumping onto aquifers, and data centers in rule-of-capture states draw groundwater with little oversight.
solution: Fuse three signals: InSAR ground deformation (seasonal elastic movement tracks aquifer drawdown), ET-based irrigation demand minus effective precipitation, and pump electricity records from cooperating utilities. Calibrate against the wells that are metered and output pumping estimates with uncertainty per parcel and month. Deliver an evidence report agencies can use in fee and compliance programs.
why_now: The NASA-ISRO NISAR radar satellite launched in mid-2025 and its L-band data is open. ET datasets have matured. California's groundwater deadlines and the Texas audit push make measurement urgent.
revenue_model: $30-200k/yr per agency or basin, plus per-report fees to lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Regulators do not need perfect meters, only defensible estimates calibrated against a sample of real ones, which is far cheaper than metering every well. The gap is that ET-only estimates cannot see storage change, and InSAR can.
first_30_days: Pick one critical-overdraft basin or Texas district with a metering plan. Reprocess two years of free Sentinel-1 InSAR, compare with the known meters, and publish a validation memo. Pitch three agencies on a 60-day paid pilot.

title: Reef Mixtapes for Oyster Hatcheries and Reefs
one_liner: Underwater speakers and a licensed library of healthy-reef soundscapes that lure oyster larvae to settle in hatchery tanks and restoration sites.
customer: Oyster hatcheries and remote-setting operations, oyster farmers, and restoration NGOs and state shellfish agencies such as those running large reef programs.
problem: Larval settlement is a costly bottleneck: eyed larvae are expensive to raise and many fail to set on cultch. Restoration reefs built on bare bottom get poor recruitment because they are silent, while healthy reefs act like acoustic beacons.
solution: A plug-in kit of a waterproof speaker, a controller and a subscription to species- and region-specific reef sound libraries recorded on healthy local reefs (snapping-shrimp crackle in the 1.5-20 kHz range). It ships with a built-in split-tank A/B protocol so any hatchery can measure the settlement gain in a week. Restoration clients can pay per acre on measured recruitment. Later products: playback buoys and acoustic tuning per species.
why_now: The science is now credible and publicised. Lab playbacks showed more oyster settlement under reef sound than under soft-bottom sound or silence (Lillis et al., PLOS ONE 2013), and later work reported large increases. In July 2026 WHOI, with The Nature Conservancy Massachusetts and shellfish constables, began a two-year effort to build a 'New England mixtape' for farmers and restorers. Rugged hydrophones and speakers are cheap. Nobody has yet packaged this for commerce.
revenue_model: Hardware kit at roughly $600-1,500, a library subscription of $50-150 per month per site, and performance-based restoration contracts (for example a share of measured settlement gains or per-acre fees). Longer term, license the sound and response dataset to acoustic-restoration players.
non_obvious_insight: Larvae navigate by ear, and degraded reefs are literally silent, so sound is a cheap cue you can sell. The defensible asset is the proprietary library of local recordings plus the settlement-response data by species and region. Commercial-hatchery effect sizes are still unproven, so the honest first product is the A/B testing rig and pay-on-results pricing, which turns scientific uncertainty into the sales pitch.
first_30_days: Buy two hydrophones and two speakers. Get three small hatcheries to run split-tank A/B settlement counts with a simple protocol, and record one healthy reef per region. Publish the first results and convert the hatcheries with the strongest lift into paying $1,500 kits.

title: Pet-Safe Demand Response With Guaranteed Temperature Floors
one_liner: A demand-response layer that ties thermostat and battery dispatch to a cheap sensor where the pet actually lives, guaranteeing a temperature floor so pet owners stop opting out of grid flexibility.
customer: Co-op and municipal utilities and VPP/DR aggregators running thermostat or battery programs, who pay per enrolled and reliably-dispatched household. Pet insurers co-fund the sensors as a heatstroke-loss and brand play.
problem: Grid flexibility is now the scarce commodity (PJM's July auction cleared at the $325/MW-day cap and came up 6.8 GW short; the Duke study found 76 GW of new load could connect with 0.25% curtailment). Thermostat DR depends on enrollment and on people not overriding events, and events land on the hottest afternoons. Roughly 95M US households own a pet, and hypothesis to test in the first month: pets are a leading reason owners opt out or override, because an animal cannot consent to 82F. Aggregators treat that as unexplained churn and lost kW.
solution: Ship a $15-25 Wi-Fi temperature/humidity sensor placed in the pet zone, integrated as a hard constraint in the dispatch engine. The engine pre-cools earlier, caps setback by heat index, and auto-releases the event if the pet-zone sensor crosses the threshold. Owners get a visible 'pet-safe' program label, and the utility gets committed kW with lower override risk. Data is shared with the insurer only with consent.
why_now: Utilities and hyperscalers are buying 'firm' distributed capacity (Sunrun/Tesla/Renew Home's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service, with no disclosed verification standard), and 25C/25D ended 12/31/2025, shifting the economics toward utility-paid flexibility. Summer 2026 heat and record affordability pressure make participation and reliability the bottleneck.
revenue_model: Per-enrolled-household fee from utilities/aggregators ($10-30 per household per year), pilot fees ($25-40K), insurer co-funding of sensors, and later performance bonuses tied to reduced override rates.
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable DR customers are the ones who currently refuse because a living creature bears the risk. A sensor-backed guarantee converts a moral veto into a contract term, and pet insurers will subsidize it because heatstroke claims are avoidable. Verify the premise cheaply against override and opt-out data before building.
first_30_days: Pitch 5 distribution co-ops (there are hundreds) and one aggregator to add a pet-owner segment to an existing thermostat program. Survey opt-outs and pull override reasons. Hand-place 100 sensors and run one event with the pet-floor rule, comparing override rates against a control. Sell a $25-40K paid pilot with the results, and approach one pet insurer for sensor co-funding.

title: Size-Glide: Reversible Tailoring for GLP-1 Wardrobes
one_liner: Prepaid mail-in take-in tailoring, done with reversible seams, that follows a GLP-1 patient down (and back up) through 3-5 sizes, sold as a retention perk to the telehealth programs that prescribe the drugs.
customer: Two payers. (1) Consumers in months 3-18 of GLP-1 treatment, mostly women 35-60 with a professional wardrobe worth $2-5k. (2) GLP-1 telehealth and employer weight-management programs, who pay a per-member fee because churn is their biggest cost.
problem: Patients drop 2-5 sizes in a year. Buying a new wardrobe at each stage costs $1-3k. Local tailors are slow, inconsistent and expensive, and permanent take-ins ruin a garment when weight comes back. Roughly half of users stop within a year and most regain, so the wardrobe problem repeats in both directions. Programs also lack a tangible, celebratory milestone reward that keeps people enrolled.
solution: A prepaid alteration bag ships to your door. A vetted network of micro-tailors runs a standardized 12-garment menu (waist, hem, darts, sleeves) using reversible methods: basted or removable seams and preserved allowances. Every garment gets a QR tag and a digital 'garment passport' recording each alteration and its size band. Weight milestones trigger reminders ('you are down 15 lb, send the blazers'). A let-out service and a resale or donate-out handoff handle regain and garments that are now too big. Telehealth partners can offer 'your first three take-ins are free' as a milestone reward.
why_now: The Wegovy pill launched in January 2026 and Lilly's oral drug is rolling out this year. GLP-1 households now command roughly $660B in spending power (Numerator, August 2026). Employer coverage and cost pressure are creating start-stop cycles, which makes reversible work the safer product.
revenue_model: Prepaid alteration packs of $250-600 per stage, or a $39-79/month wardrobe plan. B2B2C: $10-25 per member per month from telehealth and employer programs as a retention benefit. Small margin on resale handoffs.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not clothing, it is tailor turnaround and the trust that a garment can come back to its old size. Reversibility is the moat because regain is the norm, not the exception. The best paying customer is the telehealth company's churn budget, not the patient.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 alteration shops in one metro and write a 12-item price menu. Post in r/Zepbound and r/Ozempic communities and local GLP-1 clinic groups to sell 50 prepaid packs. Run a pilot with one small GLP-1 clinic or telehealth startup using free milestone take-ins. Use QR tags and a spreadsheet for the garment passport, and courier pickup for logistics.

title: Credit Union Tokenized Deposit Network
one_liner: Give thousands of small credit unions a shared 24/7 tokenized-deposit settlement network so they can answer the 'war for deposits' together instead of losing it one by one.
customer: Credit unions ($500M-$10B assets), state leagues and CUSOs, and later their members and local merchants.
problem: Banks describe the stablecoin fight as a '$6 trillion war for deposits' (CoinDesk, 2026-09-14). No single credit union has the scale to run its own token or build 24/7 settlement, and Zelle-style networks are controlled by big banks. Members get weekday-hours payments between institutions.
solution: A CUSO-owned network of tokenized member deposits (not a stablecoin at first), starting with 24/7 credit-union-to-credit-union settlement for shared branching and member P2P, then bill pay and merchant acceptance. A licensed trust-bank or custody partner handles the token layer and reserves.
why_now: The OCC charter wave (Circle 2026-07-10, Coinbase April, Bridge and Crypto.com conditional) has made compliant token infrastructure available to partner with. Citi and Coinbase launched corporate stablecoin acceptance on 2026-09-28, and the GENIUS Act takes effect around Jan 2027 (verify).
revenue_model: Network transaction fees, SaaS to member credit unions, and a share of reserve income on the settlement layer.
non_obvious_insight: The cooperative structure is the unfair advantage. Credit unions already share ATMs, branching and core processing through CUSOs, so a shared money layer is a natural extension that gives 4,500 small institutions scale none could build alone.
first_30_days: Get LOIs from five credit unions through one state league. Run a paper pilot for inter-credit-union treasury settlement with a partner trust bank, and charge pilot fees for design work and integration.

title: Recovery Audits for Downstream Tariff Refunds
one_liner: A contingency-fee recovery-audit firm that mines buyers' AP invoice history for IEEPA-era price step-ups and files contract claims against suppliers who pocketed the tariff refund.
customer: Mid-market companies that paid tariff-inflated prices but were not importer of record: hospital systems and GPOs, restaurant groups, distributors, contractors, regional retailers. They pay 20-30% of dollars recovered. Secondary buyers: importers who want a defensible refund-sharing allocation, and plaintiffs' firms that need per-customer surcharge damages.
problem: Importers stand to receive roughly $166B of IEEPA refunds. Downstream buyers who paid blended, un-itemized price increases have no easy way to size or claim their share. A commercial litigator quoted by CFO.com says his team reads hundreds of thousands of invoices by hand to compare pre-tariff and tariff-period pricing, and that many suppliers keep the refund unless asked. In parallel, at least 25 customer suits (Amazon, Costco, Walmart, Sony and others) plead unjust enrichment. Plaintiffs will need per-customer surcharge data that nobody has assembled.
solution: Ingest a buyer's AP/ERP invoice line-item export (or PDFs via extraction). Normalize SKUs and suppliers. Detect step-changes in unit price against control SKUs and commodity indices around the tariff effective dates. Infer country of origin and HTS duty exposure from public tariff tables. Estimate the IEEPA-attributable overcharge per supplier. Then generate claim packets keyed to each contract's price-adjustment, cost-pass-through or MFN clauses, with demand-letter templates and a supplier-response tracker. Start with contracts that have explicit surcharge or cost-plus language, where recovery is strongest. Partner with one or two commercial litigation boutiques for enforcement, and have human analysts review the top claims. Second product: a refund-allocation ledger for importers and distributors that want to share refunds with customers, as Williams-Sonoma and O'Reilly are doing. Third product: a damages engine for class counsel.
why_now: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February 2026. CBP's CAPE refund portal opened April 20, 2026. CBP had paid $100B by August 7, and CAPE Phase 3 for finally liquidated entries starts October 6, 2026. An Atlanta Fed survey (September 24) says most companies will hold refunds as cash. A trade court also ruled the 10% global tariff illegal on May 7, so more refund waves may follow. Contract-notice and limitation windows are running now.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered dollars. Flat $15-50k fee for importer-side allocation reports. Per-matter fees from plaintiffs' firms. Possible later add-on: an expected-value model for funds that buy refund claims.
non_obvious_insight: For downstream buyers the refund is not a customs-law problem. It is an AP-data forensics problem, the same shape as classic recovery audits (freight, telecom, sales tax), which are paid on contingency, and the recovery-audit firms have not pivoted to it. The evidence shows the gap is manual labor: CFO.com describes lawyers examining 'hundreds of thousands of invoices' to find blended tariff pricing (https://www.cfo.com/news/these-businesses-didnt-pay-tariffs-theyre-seeking-refunds-anyway-Glen-Frost-Tim-Meyer/823107/). At least 25 customer suits need per-customer surcharge data (https://www.cfodive.com/news/amazon-companies-fighting-centralized-tariff-refund-suits-costco-cfo/830814/). Refund claims are also being sold at steep discounts (American Eagle sold $68.9M of claims for $18.6M), which shows the claims are being priced without data (https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/retailers-eager-for-cash-sell-off-rights-to-potential-tariff-refunds/827064/). CBP paid $100B by August 7 (https://www.supplychaindive.com/news/cbp-has-paid-100b-in-ieepa-tariff-refunds/827257/). Main risk: B2B pass-through litigation is largely untested, so lead with contract-backed claims.
first_30_days: Pick 3 verticals with blended pricing and heavy AP volume (medical/dental supply buyers, restaurant groups, HVAC/plumbing contractors, regional grocers). Offer a free 'tariff exposure scan' from 12 months of AP export and run it on 3-5 pilot datasets. Sign a contingency engagement with a trade or commercial litigation boutique for enforcement. Build supplier claim-packet templates for the 10 most common contract clause types. Aim for the first demand letters in week 4 and first recovered dollars inside 90 days.

title: Population-Diverse iPSC Villages for Drug Safety
one_liner: Pool 50-100 genetically diverse donor iPSC lines in one dish and read out each donor's drug response by genotype, giving pharma a 'clinical trial in a dish' for roughly the cost of one experiment.
customer: Pharma safety-pharmacology and toxicology groups, oligonucleotide and gene-editing developers worried about idiosyncratic toxicity, and NAM-adopting CROs.
problem: The NAM debate centers on organ complexity, but single-donor organoids cannot show the population variability behind idiosyncratic liver injury or QT prolongation. FDA now wants 'adequately validated' methods, and conventional multi-donor testing costs n times as much.
solution: A curated, consented and commercially licensable diverse iPSC panel differentiated to cardiomyocytes or neurons (where villages are best proven), dosed with compound series and demultiplexed by genotype through scRNA-seq. Deliver donor-level dose-response distributions, genotype-linked sensitivity and concordance versus clinical outcomes.
why_now: Village-in-a-dish methods have matured, with CIRM-funded pooled iPSC-cardiomyocyte 'clinical trial in a dish' work and a 2026 methods perspective in Frontiers in Bioengineering. Greenstone Biosciences is an early commercial competitor in cardiac models. The FDA rule gives sponsors a reason to buy, and scRNA-seq costs keep falling.
revenue_model: $60-150k per compound panel, $300k/year subscriptions, and licensing the panel to CROs.
non_obvious_insight: Pooling collapses the cost of diversity: n=100 costs roughly what n=5 does. The moat is the consented, well-characterized line panel and a genotype-linked outcomes database, not the assay, which anyone can copy.
first_30_days: License 30-50 lines from public repositories, checking commercial-use consent. Build a cardiomyocyte village. Test 20 reference cardiotoxic and safe drugs and publish the concordance. Pitch 10 safety-pharmacology leads on $30k pilots.

title: Bookkeeper-Run Payee Registry Against Invoice Fraud
one_liner: Independent bookkeeping firms pool hashed vendor bank-account confirmations into a shared registry that flags fake invoices and 'new bank details' fraud at tiny businesses, then grows into a portable payment-reputation file for thin-file borrowers.
customer: Fractional bookkeeping and CFO firms serving 30-300 micro-clients ($99-500/month per firm). Later buyers are wholesalers, equipment lessors and CDFI lenders paying $3-8 per reputation pull.
problem: US payments lack payee-name verification (the UK has Confirmation of Payee; prior knowledge). AI writes flawless fake invoices and clones voices, as in Arup's roughly $25M deepfake video-call loss. Nacha's 2026 rules push originators toward risk-based fraud monitoring (prior knowledge; verify). Each bookkeeper sees only their own clients, so nobody learns from anyone else's near-miss. Separately, 22% of small firms seeking credit got nothing and solo businesses have no trade-reference file.
solution: A browser extension and API for bill-pay tools that hashes vendor name plus routing plus account and checks the registry: confirmed by N firms, flag first-time changes, and force a call-back to an independently sourced number. Confirmed payment events (on time, disputed) accrue to a per-business reputation file the owner controls and can carry between bookkeepers.
why_now: Voice cloning and AI-written invoices make payment fraud cheap. PE roll-ups of accounting firms push big players upmarket, so independent bookkeepers need shared infrastructure to compete. Bench's collapse made portability a selling point. The higher 1099 floor ($2,000 from 2026) likely means fewer W-9 and TIN collections, degrading vendor hygiene (inference).
revenue_model: $99-500/month per firm, per-pull fees from lenders and suppliers, and a revenue share back to contributing firms.
non_obvious_insight: Fraud data is a network good that big vendors cannot pool across rival software stacks, but a neutral consortium of small firms can, the way independent pharmacies and hardware stores formed co-ops. Bookkeepers already perform informal KYB on every client, so the registry monetizes knowledge they already hold.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 bookkeeping firms through a bookkeeper association or Facebook groups. Run a hashed shared registry manually (spreadsheet plus call-back desk) covering their combined 1,000+ vendors at $99/month. Record the first prevented fraud as the case study, then build the Bill.com and QuickBooks extension.

title: Visitor-Levy Back Office for Councils
one_liner: White-label registration, returns, audit and enforcement software plus a service desk that lets local councils run a new tourist levy without building it.
customer: Local authorities that have just gained the power to levy visitors: Scottish councils, Welsh councils, and Spanish, Balearic and other European municipalities.
problem: Levies are proliferating (Edinburgh in 2026, Glasgow from Jan 2027, Welsh councils from 2027, Balearics and Catalonia rising, Chicago at 19% hotel tax). Each council must register providers, collect returns, audit and chase non-payers, and most have neither software nor staff. Small B&Bs and self-caterers file badly and disputes pile up.
solution: A packaged portal for provider registration and returns, with support for per-night and percentage levies, exemptions, OTA-collected amounts and platform data feeds. It includes automated reminders, audit sampling, a provider help desk and a statutory report pack, configured per council within weeks.
why_now: New statutory levies start across the UK through 2026-27, and EU short-term rental rules require platforms to share host data with authorities from May 2026. That data can be matched against levy returns. Councils' levy revenue lets them fund administration.
revenue_model: GBP 20-60K per council per year, or a share of collected levy, plus per-return service fees for the help desk.
non_obvious_insight: Levies fail on administration rather than on rate-setting. Every council needs the same back office at the same moment, and levy revenue pays for it, so the customer has a budget line before it has a system.
first_30_days: Talk to 10 councils and the Welsh and Scottish local-government bodies. Offer a fixed-fee pilot of a provider portal and returns form for one small council. Build it from a form tool and a database first, then harden.

title: Widowhood Risk Program Sold to Medicare Payers
one_liner: Use hospice's early knowledge that a caregiver spouse is about to become a widow to enroll them in a 180-day protective program, paid for by Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs.
customer: Medicare Advantage plans (especially those with dual-eligible special needs plans), ACOs and value-based primary care groups. Hospice agencies are the intake channel and receive a referral or administrative fee.
problem: The spouse of a hospice patient is the second patient, and nobody is paid to treat them. The caregiver spouse ran the pillbox, the checkbook, the driving and the meals. They have skipped their own appointments for months. In the weeks after the funeral their chronic conditions decompensate, and hospitalizations, ED visits and falls spike. The chaplain is the one person who sees the untouched pills, the empty refrigerator and the missed doctor visits. Payers only learn of the death through enrollment data that lags by weeks or months. Hospice bereavement services are a mailing program, and they do not bill for the spouse's medical risk.
solution: A two-part program. Before the death, a hospice chaplain or social worker flags a high-risk caregiver spouse using a 6-item checklist (medication management ownership, driving, isolation, own chronic conditions, missed visits) and refers them, with consent, to the program. After the death, a community health worker does a home visit within 72 hours, books a primary care appointment within 14 days, does a medication reconciliation, sets up meal delivery and transport, and runs structured check-ins at 2 weeks, 6 weeks and 6 months. The 6-week and 6-month checks include a prolonged grief screen (PG-13-R). Screen-positive people are referred to therapists trained in prolonged grief disorder treatment, billable to insurance because PGD has had its own diagnosis code (F43.81) since October 2022.
why_now: Medicare Advantage margins are under pressure, and plans are hunting for measurable avoidable-utilization programs and star-rating improvements. Value-based primary care and ACOs are expanding, and both are rewarded for preventing ED visits and admissions. Prolonged grief disorder became an official DSM-5-TR diagnosis in 2022, with an ICD-10-CM code from October 2022, so the treatment side is finally billable. Hospices are being asked to show quality beyond death itself. I could not verify current bereavement benefit designs at specific plans, so check that before pitching.
revenue_model: A per-enrolled-spouse fee of about $150 to $300 per month for 6 months, paid by the plan or ACO. This can convert to shared savings once there are a few hundred enrollees. Hospices receive a per-referral fee or a bereavement-outsourcing fee. Therapy referrals bill insurance directly, and the program can hold a small clinician panel. Employer benefit teams are a later channel.
non_obvious_insight: The highest-risk patient is not on the payer's radar and is not the patient the hospice is paid to look after. Only the hospice team knows the caregiver is fading, and it knows months before any claim or enrollment record does. The widowhood effect (well documented in the research literature, with elevated mortality and hospitalization in the months after a spouse dies) is an underpriced, predictable utilization event.
first_30_days: Pick one regional hospice and one value-based primary care group or small MA plan with a few thousand lives. Build the checklist and a simple spreadsheet workflow, then hire one community health worker or licensed social worker. Enroll the first 20 spouses at no charge, tracking ED visits, missed PCP visits and grief screens at 90 and 180 days. Use the data to sell a paid pilot to the plan or group before month 6. Get a HIPAA lawyer to sign off on the referral pathway and consent language.

title: Walker Brain: Clip-On Sensor for Rollators
one_liner: A $60 clip-on pod that turns any walker or rollator into a fall alarm, night-light and gait-speed monitor, so there is no wearable to forget.
customer: Home-care agencies and PACE programs (buying for clients), DME suppliers, Medicare Advantage and ACO care teams, and adult children buying directly.
problem: Pendant alarms fail because many seniors won't wear them or press them. People who use walkers are among the highest fall-risk group, yet smart-walker work is mostly academic prototypes. Gait speed predicts decline and hospitalization but is measured in a clinic once a year, if at all.
solution: A clamp-on pod with an IMU, LTE-M connectivity, a small LED light strip, tip and fall detection and grip sensing. It detects when the walker is actually being used versus left by the bed at night, which is itself a leading risk signal. It auto-alerts on tipping and sends a weekly gait report and decline flags to family and the care team. Battery lasts months and the senior needs no app.
why_now: Low-power LTE-M and IMU chips are cheap. Medicare Advantage plans are measured on fall-risk management, and home-care agencies are looking for differentiation. The DME channel has not changed in decades, and the walker sensor category is still mostly prototypes.
revenue_model: Hardware $59-79, family subscription $8-12/month. B2B: about $6 per pod per month for agencies, or a per-member-per-month fee for plan pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Don't ask an 80-year-old to adopt a new device. Instrument the one object they can't give up and that is with them exactly when risk peaks. 'Walker left behind at night' is a signal no wearable can capture.
first_30_days: Prototype with off-the-shelf LTE-M dev boards and a 3D-printed clamp. Place 30 pods on walkers with 3 home-care agencies as free trials. Measure alerts and gait trends. Aim to convert 2 agencies to 100-unit pilots, and talk to outpatient physical therapists about a small validation study.

title: Portable MRI Vans for Alzheimer's Drug Safety Monitoring
one_liner: A mobile low-field MRI service that scans anti-amyloid patients at home or in memory-care communities for brain-swelling safety checks.
customer: Memory clinics, neurology practices and infusion centers running anti-amyloid therapy, plus health systems. Later, manufacturer patient-support programs and payers.
problem: Anti-amyloid drugs require serial MRI safety monitoring for ARIA (brain swelling or bleeding). Scheduling MRI slots is a hidden throttle, and frail 80-year-olds struggle with hospital scanner visits. With blood tests and at-home dosing widening the funnel, monitoring capacity is the next bottleneck.
solution: A tech plus a portable FDA-cleared low-field scanner (Hyperfine Swoop class) in a van or cart, with teleradiology reads scheduled around dosing. Start with a concordance study against 3T for ARIA-E and ARIA-H (early reports suggest low-field can flag such changes, but it needs validation), then contract per scan to clinics.
why_now: Leqembi Q1 sales rose 74% to $168M, with Eisai and Biogen expecting over $1B this year, a subcutaneous at-home starting dose is now cleared, and two blood tests are cleared. Portable MRI and AI reconstruction have matured.
revenue_model: Per-scan fee of about $250-450 paid by clinics or manufacturer support programs, a per-patient monitoring program subscription, and data licensing for post-marketing studies.
non_obvious_insight: The market talks about drug and diagnosis, but scan capacity and patient logistics decide throughput. The regulatory and reimbursement path is uncertain, so the study itself is the first product and creates the evidence moat.
first_30_days: Contact five memory clinics with anti-amyloid volume, lease a portable scanner, design a 40-patient concordance study with an IRB and neuroradiologists, and ask the drug makers' patient-support programs for pilot funding.

title: Seasonal Staff Housing from Banned Rentals
one_liner: Master-lease flats stranded by short-term-rental bans and sublet them by the bed, with employer-guaranteed rent, to short-staffed hotels in the same destination.
customer: Hotels, resorts and restaurant groups with 50-400 seasonal staff in Palma, Ibiza, Barcelona coast and similar hotspots (start in the Balearics). Secondary customer: small owners whose licences are ending.
problem: Insiders frame STR bans as residents versus tourists, with owners as the losers. The overlooked fact is that banned owners have empty flats and fear 12-month tenancy law, while the hotel next door cannot hire because staff cannot find housing. Nobody sits in the middle to handle leases, furnishing, inspections and deposits.
solution: An asset-light intermediary signs 6-11 month leases with owners under a structure vetted by local counsel. The hotel guarantees the rent and places its own staff. We handle furnishing, house rules, inspections and optional payroll-deduction of rent, and charge per bed. The wedge is one Palma pilot with 3 hotels and about 30 flats.
why_now: Palma has a full ban, Barcelona bans all STRs in Nov 2028 after Spain's top court upheld it in Oct 2025, and Madrid restricts listings. Spain fined Airbnb $75M in Dec 2025, so the stranded supply is real. Spain still had about 97M visitors, so hotels are staffing to record demand.
revenue_model: A 12-18% management fee on rent, or a EUR 40-70 per bed per month spread, plus a placement fee from the hotel and a fee for guaranteeing rent to the owner.
non_obvious_insight: A ban strands supply as well as demand, and the best tenant for that supply is the employer of the people who service tourism. Employer-guaranteed rent is better credit than any nomad or mid-term tenant, which lets owners accept lower rents for zero vacancy risk.
first_30_days: Contact HR and operations heads at 15 hotels through the Mallorca hoteliers' federation and LinkedIn, and sign 3 letters of intent for 10-20 beds each. Recruit 30 owners through ex-STR property managers and owner groups. Pay a local lawyer EUR 3-5K for a lease template. Sign leases only after the hotel LOIs are in.

title: Workout GC for Stalled Spec Homes
one_liner: A finish-the-house crew and re-sequencing service sold to construction lenders, not builders, for homes stuck at 40-90% complete.
customer: Community banks, credit unions and private construction lenders with spec-home loans being extended (Texas, Florida, Southeast, Mountain West). Secondary customer: distressed small builders referred by those lenders.
problem: Starts hold at 1.275M SAAR but completions fell 27.1% YoY. One executive described 15-20 houses stuck on foundations for 6+ weeks, and a West Virginia builder risks about 40 closings. The builder cannot get crews back, and the lender holds the real risk: exhausted interest reserves, mechanic's liens, extensions, and half-built collateral. Lenders have no operating arm.
solution: Start with a flat-fee stuck-loan triage: site visit, photo scan, cost-to-finish, days of carry and sub availability, ranked across the lender's watchlist. Then take over scheduling and finishing on cost-plus. A few in-house supers plus a pre-vetted bench of framing, MEP and finish subs are paid in 7 days through the lender's normal draw process. The builder keeps the lot and the sale. A bonus is paid per day saved before the extension deadline.
why_now: Completions are down 27.1% while starts hold. 63% of builders already use incentives and 35% cut prices, so there is no margin left to absorb delay. ICE arrests rose from 32,545 in May to 49,571 in July 2026 and are pulling crews off sites. 2027 starts are forecast down 2-4%, so more small builders will stall. The 2024-25 vintage of spec construction loans is maturing now.
revenue_model: $2.5K per-loan triage or $15K portfolio review. Finishing work at cost plus 12-15%. Success fee of about 1% of loan balance for closing before the extension deadline.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone frames stalled homes as a builder or labor problem. The party with the budget, the legal leverage and no ego is the lender, who cares about loan resolution rather than building. Subs return when someone credible promises six straight days of work and pays in a week. A lender-backed GC has that payment credibility and the stalled builder does not.
first_30_days: Call 15 construction lenders and workout officers through state bankers associations. Offer two banks a free 10-loan triage. Hire two ex-superintendents. Line up 3 framing, MEP and finish subs per metro on a 7-day-pay promise. Target a first paid contract on 1-3 homes by day 30.
